topic: Tyres as the only change on the same car: skidpad g, 60-0 or 70-0 mph braking distance and lap time on all-season against summer against track-day (200 treadwear or R-compound) tyres

cases.car: 2017 Ford Fusion Sport (engine and transmission not given in the search summary; two nearly identically optioned cars, see note)
cases.change: Factory all-season tyres replaced by the optional summer performance tyres; nothing else changed on the spec

physical.tyreBefore: all-season (model and size not given in summary)
physical.tyreAfter: summer performance tyre option (model and size not given in summary)
physical.stabilityControl: inhibited for the 0.89 g summer-tyre skidpad run

cases.measure: Car and Driver instrumented test: steady-state skidpad lateral g (skidpad diameter not stated in the summary) and 70-0 mph braking distance
cases.publisher: Car and Driver (syndicated on Yahoo News: '2017 Ford Fusion Sport with Performance Tires')
cases.note: Summary wording: 'The summer tires helped the Sport generate 0.89 g on the skidpad, 0.05 g greater than with the all-seasons' (all-season car measured at 0.84 g; the 0.89 g figure was taken with stability control inhibited) and 'The summer tires chop 23 feet off the 70-mph-to-zero stopping distance, the deed having been done in 155 feet.' The all-season 70-0 figure of 178 ft is not printed in the summary: it is 155 ft plus the stated 23 ft. The summer tyres also cost one-tenth of a second in both 0-60 mph and the quarter-mile (absolute times not in summary, not recorded). The summary says Car and Driver tested 'a nearly identically optioned 2017 Fusion Sport with the summer-tire fitment rather than the same car on both tire sets', so before and after are two cars of the same spec, not one car. A Michelin fitment page in the results lists 235/40R19 96V for the 2017 Fusion Sport (URL only; not confirmed as the test tyre size). Read from search-result summary; page not opened. Second reader: a later summary of the same syndicated pieces quotes the all-season stop directly ('Stopping from 70 mph took an acceptable 178 feet; the optional ($195) summer-only tire chops the braking distance to just 155 feet') and says the car is 'still stability-control-inhibited on the skidpad'.
cases.checkNote: A second search summary of the Car and Driver pieces states 178 ft (all-season) and 155 ft (summer, a $195 option) from 70 mph and 0.84 against 0.89 g directly, but before and after are two nearly identically optioned cars, not one car.

cases.car: 2009 Honda Civic Si (named by the second reader's search summary), sold from the factory with a choice of same-size all-season or summer tyres (215/45R17), the summer tyre a $200 option
cases.change: Michelin Pilot HX MXM4 all-season replaced by Michelin Pilot Exalto PE2 summer tyre, same size, same car; a snow tyre (181 ft) was also tested

physical.tyreBefore: Michelin Pilot HX MXM4 all-season, 215/45R17 (treadwear grade not in summary)
physical.tyreAfter: Michelin Pilot Exalto PE2 summer, 215/45R17 (treadwear grade not in summary)

cases.measure: Edmunds instrumented test: 60-0 mph braking distance on the same car with each tyre, very probably on the purpose-built wet surface (see note); not a dry-grip figure
cases.publisher: Edmunds ('Tire Test: All-Season vs. Snow vs. Summer')
cases.note: Summary wording: 'the summer tire's 157-foot stop is the shortest, the snow tires come up 2nd at 181 feet and the all-season tires lag further behind in a flurry of ABS activity on the way to a distance of 215 feet'; 'The snow tire's 12.7-second effort for 2nd place is significantly better, but the summer tire tops them all with an 11.9-second performance' (all-season 15.4 s). The test car 'can be bought with your choice of Michelin Pilot HX MXM4 all-season tires or, for $200 more, Michelin Pilot Exalto PE2 high-performance summer tires, both in size 215/45R17.' On the wet skidpad the summer tyre reached 0.81 g; the all-season skidpad figure was not in any summary, so skidpad is not recorded. Surface is uncertain: one summary mentions the 'wet skid pad', another says the test was on a snowy surface, which sits badly with the summer tyre beating the snow tyre. The 0-60 times and stops are far longer than dry figures for any ordinary car, so this is a low-grip-surface result and must not be used to check dry grip. Read from search-result summary; page not opened. Second reader: the 157/181/215 ft stops are confirmed by a second summary. The 11.9 s and 12.7 s times are WET 0-40 mph acceleration on a purpose-built wet surface, not 0-60 ('the summer tire posted an 11.9-second run, over 20 percent quicker than the all-season tire'), and another summary gave a conflicting all-season acceleration time (22.9 s, snow 19.1 s), so the acceleration fields were removed. The article then says 'Things are much the same when braking from 60 mph', which places the 60-0 stops on the wet surface; in the separate snow test the summer tyre needed 351 ft, 'almost double' the all-season distance on snow, so tyre ranking flips with surface.
cases.checkNote: Corrected: car identified as a 2009 Honda Civic Si, the 15.4/11.9 s figures were wet 0-40 mph times mislabelled as 0-60 (removed), and the confirmed 215/157 ft 60-0 stops are wet-surface results.

cases.measure: Car and Driver instrumented test: 300-ft skidpad lateral g and 70-0 mph braking distance
cases.publisher: Car and Driver (syndicated on AOL: 'We Fix Ford's Mistake by Fitting the Maverick Lobo with Summer Tires, and It Pays Off in Our Tests')
cases.note: Added by the second reader. Summary wording: 'the Lobo's lateral grip rose from 0.85 to 0.90 g around our 300-foot skidpad'; 'reduced the Lobo's stopping distance by 24 feet, from 188 feet to 164 feet at 70 mph'; from 100 mph 'shrinking the requirement from 378 to 337 feet'. Noise rose from 23 to 24 sones at 70 mph. The summary implies the same truck on both sets but does not state it, and gives no tyre sizes, so a size change cannot be ruled out. 70-0 gain 12.8%. Read from search-result summary; page not opened.
cases.checkNote: Added from a single syndicated Car and Driver summary with clear before/after figures; no independent second source was searched and tyre sizes are not given.

ruleOfThumb.claim: Summer tyres typically offer better steering precision, shorter braking distances and higher cornering limits than all-season tyres (qualitative, no figure).
ruleOfThumb.note: Summary: 'summer tires typically offer better steering precision, shorter braking distances, and higher cornering limits.' A buying guide, not a controlled result. Read from search-result summary; page not opened.

ruleOfThumb.claim: Summer tyres stop 10-20% shorter than all-season tyres (attributed to Tire Rack by a tyre retailer; attribution not confirmed).
ruleOfThumb.note: The search summary says the blog 'gives a 10-20% braking advantage for summer tires and attributes it to Tire Rack' but that the attribution could not be confirmed. Against this page: the Car and Driver Fusion Sport 70-0 stop was 12.9% shorter on summer tyres and the Maverick Lobo 70-0 stop 12.8% shorter (both inside the range); the Edmunds wet 60-0 result was 27% shorter (outside it). Read from search-result summary; page not opened.

ruleOfThumb.claim: Modern performance all-season tyres can come close to summer tyres: a 2026 Corvette E-Ray on all-season tyres averaged 1.01 g on Car and Driver's 300-ft skidpad, the first car to pass 1.0 g on all-seasons, and gave up very little to Pilot Sport 4S summer tyres, needing about one extra foot to stop.
ruleOfThumb.publisher: Corvette Blogger, reporting a Car and Driver test
ruleOfThumb.note: Summary: the E-Ray 'equipped with all-season rubber circled Car and Driver's 300-foot skidpad with a 1.01-g average'; per a secondary summary 'the stock Michelin All-Seasons gave up very little in performance to the Pilot Sport 4S summer tires, and the car needed just one extra foot in braking'. Not recorded as a case: no summer-tyre skidpad figure and no absolute braking distances were in the summaries. Read from search-result summary; page not opened.

ruleOfThumb.claim: 200-treadwear track tyres do not necessarily slow down as they wear: in a long-term Super 200 test a Vitour P1 ran the same lap times new at 7/32 in and worn to 4/32 in, while a Nankang CR-S ran clearly quicker with less tread.
ruleOfThumb.note: Summary: 'The Vitour P1 delivered the same lap times both when new at 7/32 inch and when worn to 4/32, yet the Nankang CR-S clearly ran much quicker with less tread.' Lap times themselves were not in the summary. Read from search-result summary; page not opened.

ruleOfThumb.claim: On an autocross, a 200-treadwear tyre (BFGoodrich Rival S) ran about 1.8 s quicker than a street tyre on the same C5 Corvette Z06, while peak lateral grip was very similar across the tyres; the differences showed over the run.
ruleOfThumb.publisher: Grassroots Motorsports (Project C5 Corvette Z06 Part 5)
ruleOfThumb.note: Added by the second reader. Summary: the BFGoodrich R1 S posted the day's best time of 27.703 s; the Rival S was about 1.8 s quicker than the street tire; lateral grip peaks were very similar across all three tyres. Not recorded as a case: the street tyre's model and the per-tyre absolute times were not in the summary. Read from search-result summary; page not opened.
